title: Breaking Bad News to a Key Client
titleEs: Dar una mala noticia a un cliente clave
summary: Tell a key client what they did not want to hear and keep their trust: a brief warning, the news in one clear sentence, a short reason without blame, your share of responsibility (a mixed conditional helps), and a plan with dates. Hedge the warning and the reason, never the decision.
canDo: Break bad news in five moves: warning, news, reason, ownership and plan.
State a decision firmly (*will not be*) and keep the softness for the warning, the empathy and the reason.
Use *would* for rejected alternatives, a mixed conditional for ownership and *will* for commitments.
Say *let her know* and *hear it from me* with their weak forms, and *unfortunately*, *disappointing* and *go live* with the right stress and vowels.

focus.grammar: Integration: firm will / will not for decisions and commitments · would for rejected alternatives (a rushed fix would…) · mixed conditional for ownership (if we had tested…, we would be… now) · hedges only in the warning and the reason · in the meantime + will
focus.lexis: I'm afraid I have some disappointing news, I wanted you to hear it from me, as we discussed, that's a blow, count on, be straight with someone, we regret to inform you, in the meantime, put something at risk, accordingly, go live, hate to tell you this
focus.afh: weak forms with h-dropping: let her know /ˈlet̬‿ɚ/ · from /frəm/ in hear it from me · unFORtunately /ʌnˈfɔːr.tʃən.ət.li/ · disapPOINTing · go live /laɪv/, not /lɪv/

warmup: Think of a time you received bad news from a company: a cancelled flight, a delayed order, a price increase. What made it worse: the news itself, the timing, or the way they told you?

scenario.title: Search: decision and next steps
scenario.context: Friday afternoon. Ryan has called Helen to give her the decision. Now he confirms it in writing, so she can share it with her board.
scenario.speaker: ryan
scenario.text: Dear Helen, thank you for your time on the phone this morning. {{As we discussed}}, the full search {{will not be}} part of the go-live on June 20. I realize this is {{disappointing}}, especially for your board. Our full-scale test showed that the search cannot yet handle peak traffic, and a rushed fix {{would put}} the rest of the launch {{at risk}}. {{If we had tested}} at full scale earlier, we {{would be}} in a better position now, and we have changed our test plan for phase two {{accordingly}}. {{In the meantime}}, customers will have the basic search with an invoice-number filter on day one, and the full search will {{go live}} in the July update. I will send you a one-page summary for your board by Wednesday. Kind regards, Ryan

organizer.title: Five sentences, five moves
organizer.prompt: Name the move of each sentence: warning, news, reason, ownership or plan.
rows: I'm afraid I have some disappointing news about the search.
The full search will not be part of the go-live on June 20.
A rushed fix would put the rest of the launch at risk.
If we had tested at full scale earlier, we would be in a better position now.
In the meantime, customers will have the basic search on day one.
organizer.explain: Warning → news → reason → ownership → plan. The news comes in the second sentence, not after the explanation.

questions.q: On Tuesday the team wrote *the search may not be ready*. Now Ryan says *the full search will not be part of the go-live*. Why has the hedge disappeared? Which parts of the text are still soft, and why?
questions.model: On Tuesday the decision had not been taken, so *may not* matched the real uncertainty. Now it has been taken, and hedging it (*might not*) would give Helen false hope and make the team sound unsure. The news and the plan are firm (*will not be*, *will have*, *will go live*). The soft parts are the warning (*I'm afraid I have some disappointing news*), which prepares Helen, and the reason, given with *would* (an imagined rushed fix that will not happen) and a mixed conditional, which explains without arguing.
criteria: You said the hedge disappeared because the decision is now made.
You said hedging a decision would give false hope or sound unsure.
You said the warning and the reason stay soft (*I'm afraid*, *would*, the conditional).

questions.q: Find the verb form in each move: the news, the reason, the ownership sentence and the plan. Why does each move use the form it uses?
questions.model: The news: *will not be*, a firm future fact. The reason: *would put*, the imagined result of an alternative the team has rejected (a rushed fix). Ownership: a mixed conditional, *if we had tested* (unreal past) + *we would be… now* (its present effect). The plan: *will have*, *will go live*, firm commitments. Rule of thumb: *will* for what is decided or promised, *would* for what you imagine and reject.
criteria: You identified *will not be* for the news and *will have / will go live* for the plan.
You identified *would put* for the rejected alternative.
You identified the mixed conditional (*had tested… would be… now*) for ownership.

questions.q: Helen ends the call with *I'd rather hear it now than on launch day. Thank you for being straight with me.* What did Ryan do that made her react like this, even though the news is bad? Think about the timing, the order of the moves and what he offered her for her board.
questions.model: Ryan gave the news early (after a warning on Tuesday and well before launch day), by phone before writing, and in his own words. He warned her, gave the news in one clear sentence, explained briefly without blaming anyone, owned the team's part and offered a plan with dates. He also thought about her next problem, the board: a one-page summary she can share helps her pass the news upwards. Bad news damages relationships when it arrives late, vague or wrapped in excuses; delivered like this, it builds trust.
criteria: You mentioned the timing: early, after a first warning, by phone before email.
You mentioned the clear order: warning, news in one sentence, no blame, ownership, plan.
You mentioned that he helped with her next conversation (the summary for the board).

points: Bad news in five moves: a short warning (*I'm afraid I have some disappointing news*) → the news in one clear sentence → a brief reason, without blame → ownership of your part → the plan, with dates.
Once a decision is made, state it firmly (*will not be*). Hedging a decision gives false hope. Keep the softness for the warning, the empathy and the reason.

Use *would* for the alternatives you rejected (*a rushed fix would put the launch at risk*), a mixed conditional to own the past (*if we had tested earlier, we would be… now*) and *will* for commitments.
Think about the client's next conversation and give them something to share (*a one-page summary for your board*).
formulas: I'm afraid I have some disappointing news about + noun · X will not be + …
a rushed / different option would + verb · If we had + past participle, we would + bare infinitive + now
In the meantime, … will + verb · I'll send you + noun + by + day
rule.note: Spanish politeness often delays bad news with context. In English business culture, the news comes in the first or second sentence, after a brief warning. A long delay makes the listener anxious, and they may suspect you are hiding something.

phonetics.intro: Al dar malas noticias por teléfono, la claridad depende también del ritmo. Los pronombres y preposiciones átonos se reducen tanto que la h desaparece: *let her know* suena «LÉ-rər-NOU», y *from* se convierte en «frəm». Además, tres palabras clave tienen trampas para el hispanohablante: el acento de *unfortunately* y *disappointing*, y la vocal de *live* en *go live*.

alerts.text: *Her* sin acento pierde la h y se reduce a /ɚ/ (US) o /ə/ (UK): «LÉ-rər». Igual *him* /ɪm/ y *them* /ðəm/: *tell him* «TÉ-lim».
En EE. UU., la t de *let* entre vocales es una r simple: «LÉ-rər-NOU». En Reino Unido, t suave: «LÉ-tə».
La h vuelve cuando *her* abre la frase o se enfatiza: *Her board was counting on it* /hɚ/.

alerts.text: Aquí *live* es adjetivo: /laɪv/, «laiv», como en *a live concert*. No /lɪv/, «liv», que es el verbo *vivir*.
La v final es sonora, /v/: los dientes de arriba sobre el labio de abajo, con vibración. No «laif».

l1.title: Inform without the person
l1.text: *Inform* needs the person: *inform you that…*, *inform the board of…*.

l1.right: We regret to inform you that the search will not be ready.

l1.title: Sorry for the inconveniences
l1.text: *Inconvenience* is usually uncountable in apologies, and *any* sounds more natural than *the*.

l1.title: The story before the news

task.title: Breaking new bad news to Helen
task.scenario: Early July. The full search is on track for the July update, but there is new bad news. Oliver has just sent you his notes on the reports page: the supplier's live data feed will not be ready until mid-August. Turn Oliver's notes into an email to Helen. She has not heard anything yet, and her board meets next week.
task.brief: Mediate from a colleague's technical notes to a client email: warning, news, reason, ownership and plan.

input.title: Oliver's notes on the reports page
input.speaker: oliver
input.text: Ryan, quick notes on the reports. The supplier's live feed won't be ready until 15 August; they told us yesterday. Their new format is still changing, so we can't build against it yet. What we can do: show data up to the end of the previous month, refreshed every Monday. Customers lose real-time figures, but nothing else breaks. Honestly, if we'd asked them to confirm the format in writing back in May, we'd have the live data now. I can have the weekly refresh running by Friday.
input.tts: Ryan, quick notes on the reports. The supplier's live feed won't be ready until the fifteenth [of](/əv/) August; they told us yesterday. Their new format is still changing, so we can't build against it yet. What we [can](/kən/) do: show data up to the end [of](/əv/) the previous month, refreshed every Monday. Customers lose real-time figures, [but](/bət/) nothing else breaks. Honestly, if we'd asked them to confirm the format in writing back in May, we'd have the live data now. I [can](/kən/) have the weekly refresh running by Friday.

steps: Warn Helen in one sentence that bad news is coming.
Give the news in one clear sentence, with the date.
Give the reason briefly, without blaming the supplier.
Own your part with a mixed conditional (*if we had… we would… now*).
Give the plan with *will* and dates, and offer something for her board.

parts.label: Bad news to a key client (neutral-formal email)
notes: *I'm afraid I have some disappointing news about the reports page*: the warning, in the first sentence, and it names the area.
*Live data will not be available until 15 August*: the news, firm and dated, in the second sentence.
*The supplier's new data format is still changing*: the reason as a fact, without blame. Oliver's *they told us yesterday* is left out: it adds nothing for Helen.

*If we had asked them to confirm the format in writing in May, we would have the live data now*: Oliver's *if we'd asked…, we'd have…* in written form; the team owns its part and says what has changed.
*In the meantime… will show… starting this Friday* and *I will send you a short note for your board*: firm commitments, plus help with her next conversation.
